title: The teacher's curled fingers
hook: a teacher's hand curled closed, a student's promises, and the book that says the highest reality is a person
carry: brahman is a person: vishnu, to know and love

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: the Tamil Veda, holy words in the people's tongue. Ten verses led Nathamuni to a thousand, and a lost Tamil Veda was handed back, through a line of teachers that would reach Ramanuja.
screen: `THE TAMIL VEDA, FOUND AGAIN.` · `TODAY: RAMANUJA'S BOOK.`

segments.voice: A hand, curled closed. The Sri Vaishnava tradition says that when the young Ramanuja hurried to meet the great teacher Yamuna, he arrived too late. Yamuna had died, and some fingers of his hand were curled tight, as if holding on to something. Those around him read them as wishes left undone. Ramanuja stood by the body and made promises aloud, and with each one, the story says, a finger straightened. One of those promises was a book: the Sri Bhashya.
screen: `A HAND, CURLED CLOSED.` → `A PROMISE FOR EACH FINGER.` → `ONE OF THEM WAS A BOOK.`

segments.voice: The promise was a commentary on the Brahma Sutras, and the student kept it. The Brahma Sutras are tiny, packed lines, too short to understand alone. A bhashya is a commentary that opens them up, line by line. And the Sri Bhashya argues in the open. Again and again Ramanuja sets out the opposing view first, in full, as if a sharp rival were sitting across from him, and only then answers. Indian commentaries call that the purvapaksha, the prior view. Among his opponents are other Vedanta teachers, and he gives their arguments at length before replying. And what does he argue for? This is the big teaching, and it has a name: Vishishtadvaita, often translated qualified non-dualism. Brahman, the one reality the Upanishads point to, isn't a faceless force. Brahman is a person, Narayana, Vishnu, full of every good quality and free of every fault. The world is real. Each self is real, and never apart from God. That's why Sri Vaishnava families can call the highest reality by name, sing to him and serve him in the temple: the God the philosophers argue about and the God the Alvars sang to are one and the same. Theology, in this book, means thinking hard about a God you can also love. Over the next days, a few of its pieces, one at a time.
screen: `A PROMISE TO A TEACHER'S HAND.` · `THE OTHER VIEW FIRST.` · `BRAHMAN IS A PERSON: VISHNU.` · `A GOD TO THINK ABOUT, AND LOVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one question about God or faith where someone close to you sees it differently: a parent, a friend, a partner. First, the way Ramanuja did, say their view in your head as well as you can, in full, as if you were defending it, and stay there a few breaths. Then let your own view come back, and notice whether it has changed shape. If you pray, end by calling the One you pray to by name; if you don't, end by naming what you most hope is true.
Vaishnava theology. Today, Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya: the other view first, then his answer. Brahman is a person, Vishnu, to think about and to love.
Your line: Brahman is a person: Vishnu, to know and love. A promise at a teacher's side became the book that says so. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: In the Sri Vaishnava tradition, the Sri Bhashya is studied with a teacher, often alongside its later commentaries, and students learn its method: set out the opposing view in full, then answer it from the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutras.

fork.setup: you're Ramanuja, standing by your teacher's body, some of his fingers curled closed. what do you do?
options: leave quietly; it's too late now.
promise aloud to finish what he hoped for.
start a school of your own and forget the rest.
fork.reveal: the story says Ramanuja made promises aloud, one of them a commentary on the Brahma Sutras, and with each one a finger straightened.

original.note: Sanskrit: Ramanuja's commentary on the Brahma Sutras, the core text of Sri Vaishnava theology.

notes: Editor: the writer's hook told the Tirukoshtiyur temple-tower story, already told in year one (day 289) and recalled on day 290; the hook now opens on Yamuna's curled fingers (moved up from the teach), and the fork and a match pair no longer use the tower. The review now picks up the re-angled day 1225 (Nathamuni and the ten verses). 'His rivals are other Vedanta teachers' became 'among his opponents' (the Sri Bhashya also answers non-Vedanta schools); 'in its strongest form' became 'in full'.
The curled-fingers story is told as tradition; the number of fingers and the other promises are deliberately left out ('some fingers', 'one of those promises').
Thibaut's 1904 English translation of the Sri Bhashya (Sacred Books of the East 48) exists but is not on the public-domain list the validator knows, so nothing is quoted.

The summary of the Sri Bhashya's claims (Brahman as Narayana with all good qualities and no faults; the world and selves real and inseparable; the scriptures in harmony) should be checked by a Sri Vaishnava Keeper.
